unit.unitTitle: Getting Help and Getting Things Done
unit.unitOverview: The last teaching unit of Level 1, and it is about the language that turns a problem into a fixed problem. Describing a fault precisely, saying why you want something so the other person can help you properly, and getting through a form without being defeated by the four boxes that catch everybody. It ends with a real form and a real complaint, because those are the two documents where imprecise English costs the most.
unit.learningPath:
Read and listen to the Lesson. There are three patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 1 is vocabulary that behaves like grammar — precision is the whole point.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a form and a written complaint.
Do the Practice. Practice 1 is the one that changes what you get.
Record yourself reporting three faults and making an appointment.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
Last teaching unit of Level 1, and it is a practical one. Everything here is about getting something fixed, arranged or approved.
First pattern: describing what is wrong. This looks like vocabulary and it behaves like grammar, because the words are not interchangeable and choosing the wrong one sends the wrong person.
There are five sentences and they mean different things.
It doesn't work. Nothing happens at all. It is completely dead.
It isn't working. Nothing is happening at the moment. Slightly softer, and it suggests the problem might be temporary.
It's broken. Something is physically damaged. There is a part that has failed.
There's something wrong with it. Something is not right, and you do not know what. This is the honest one when you genuinely do not know.
It's not working properly. It works, but not correctly. This is the one people forget, and it is the most common real situation — the thing runs, but it does something wrong.
Why does this matter? Because whoever helps you decides what to do based on your sentence. It's broken sends somebody with parts. It's not working properly sends somebody to look at settings. If you say broken when you mean not working properly, the wrong person comes, and you wait again.
And then the three details that turn a report into an actionable one.
What exactly happens. Not it's broken, but it stops after about a minute.
When it started. Since Tuesday. Since the power cut.
What you have already tried. I've switched it off and on. That saves the other person from asking you to do the thing you have already done, which is the first thing they will suggest.
Problem, since when, already tried. Three pieces, and a report with all three gets a different response from one with none.
Second pattern: so that.
In Unit 13 you learned because and so. Because gives a reason. So gives a result.
So that is different from both. It gives a purpose — why you are doing something, what you want to achieve.
I'm writing so that you have it in writing.
I'd like an early appointment so that I don't miss work.
Can you confirm by email so that I have a record?
Notice the difference from so on its own. It was raining, so we stayed at home — that is a result, something that happened. I'm leaving early so that I catch the train — that is a purpose, something I want to happen.
A simple test: if you can put in order to instead, it is so that. In order to catch the train. You cannot say it was raining in order to we stayed at home.
And here is why this small structure is worth a whole card. When you ask for something and give the purpose, you get a much better answer. Can I have an early appointment is a request somebody can say no to. Can I have an early appointment so that I don't miss work gives them something to work with — and if the early one is not available, they will often find you a different solution to the same problem. The purpose is more useful than the request.
Third pattern: forms and appointments.
Forms are mostly vocabulary, and four boxes catch almost everybody.
Surname is your family name. First name is your given name. Different countries put these in different orders, and forms want them in their own boxes, so read the labels rather than the order.
Occupation means your job. It does not mean your employer.
Delete as applicable means cross out the ones that do not apply to you and leave the one that does. It looks like an instruction to delete something and it is the opposite of a choice — you are removing the wrong answers.
Block capitals means write in large separate letters, not joined. Forms ask for this so a machine or a stranger can read your handwriting.
And two habits. Read the whole form before writing anything, because the last question often changes an earlier answer. And if a box does not apply, write N/A rather than leaving it blank — a blank looks like you forgot, and it comes back.
For appointments, there is a fixed order, exactly like the ticket window in Unit 10.
What you need. When you are available. Whether it is urgent. And then your details.
I'd like to make an appointment about a leak. I'm available any morning this week. It's not urgent but it is getting worse.
That last part is the one people leave out and it is the one that decides when you are seen.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: Five Ways to Say It Is Wrong
readings.passageScript:
There are five common ways to say something is wrong in English and they are not interchangeable. Choosing between them decides who comes to help you.
It doesn't work. Nothing happens at all. Completely dead.
It isn't working. Nothing is happening at the moment. Softer, and it hints the problem might be temporary.
It's broken. Something is physically damaged. A part has failed.
There's something wrong with it. Something is not right and you do not know what. This is the honest one, and there is no shame in it.
It's not working properly. It works, but incorrectly. This is the one people forget and it describes the most common real situation — the thing runs, and does the wrong thing.
Why does the choice matter? Because the person you tell decides what to do next based on your sentence, and they usually decide before speaking to you again.
It's broken sends somebody with parts and tools.
It's not working properly sends somebody to look at settings.
If you say broken when you mean not working properly, the wrong person arrives, cannot help, and you go back on the list.
Then there are three details that turn a description into something actionable.
What exactly happens. Not it's broken, but it stops after about a minute.
When it started. Since Tuesday. Since the power cut.
What you have already tried. I've switched it off and on again.
That third one is the most underrated sentence in this whole unit. Without it, the first thing you will be asked to do is the thing you have already done, and the conversation restarts.

readings.title: Say Why, Not Just What
readings.passageScript:
There is a small structure that changes how much help you get, and it costs four words.
So that gives a purpose. It answers why you want something, rather than what you want.
Can I have an early appointment?
Can I have an early appointment so that I don't miss work?
The first is a request that can be refused with one word. The second gives the other person something to work with.
Here is what actually happens. If the early appointment does not exist, the answer to the first question is no, and the conversation ends. The answer to the second is often something else entirely — we don't have anything early, but there's a late one at six, would that work? They have solved your problem rather than answered your question, and they could only do that because you told them what the problem was.
This generalises. When you ask for something, the request is your guess at a solution. The purpose is the actual need. People can nearly always help with a need; they can only say yes or no to a guess.
So that is different from the so you learned in Unit 13. So gives a result — it was raining, so we stayed at home. That already happened. So that gives a purpose — I'm leaving early so that I catch the train. That has not happened yet, and it is what I want.
The test is short: if in order to fits, it is so that. In order to catch the train works. In order to we stayed at home does not.
One caution. A purpose is useful and an explanation is not the same thing. So that I don't miss work is a purpose. A long account of your week is an explanation, and it makes the request harder to say yes to rather than easier. One clause is enough.

REPAIR REQUEST FORM
  Northfield Housing - Section A

  SURNAME     ...............  (block capitals)
  FIRST NAME  ...............
  ADDRESS     ...............
  POSTCODE    ...............
  OCCUPATION  ...............

  Mr / Ms / Mx   (delete as applicable)

  NATURE OF PROBLEM  (tick ONE box only)
    [ ] Heating      [ ] Water
    [ ] Electrical   [ ] Structural
    [ ] Other .......................

  IS THIS URGENT?   (tick all that apply)
    [ ] Risk to safety
    [ ] Getting worse
    [ ] No hot water
    [ ] None of these

  DESCRIPTION  ....................

  SIGNATURE ..........  DATE ........

  Section B is for office use only.
  Forms without a signature are returned
  unprocessed. Allow 10 working days.

-----------------------------------------

  COMPLAINT - sent 3 weeks later

  Dear Repairs Team,

  I reported a leak under the kitchen sink
  on 4 March (reference NH-8841). An
  engineer visited on 11 March and said a
  part was needed. I have heard nothing
  since.

  The leak is now worse and the cupboard
  floor is damaged.

  I am writing so that there is a record of
  the delay, and so that the damage is on
  file before it gets worse.

  I would like two things: a date for the
  part to be fitted, and confirmation of
  who will repair the cupboard floor.

  Please reply by 1 April.

  Yours faithfully,
  A. Bello

grammar.title: Five ways to say something is wrong
grammar.explanation: This looks like vocabulary and behaves like grammar, because the five are not interchangeable and the one you choose decides who comes to help you.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
IT DOESN'T WORK.
  Nothing happens at all. Completely dead.

IT ISN'T WORKING.
  Nothing at the moment. Softer; may be
  temporary.

IT'S BROKEN.
  Physically damaged. A part has failed.

THERE'S SOMETHING WRONG WITH IT.
  Not right, and you don't know what.
  The honest one.

IT'S NOT WORKING PROPERLY.
  It works, but incorrectly.
  The most common real situation.

WHY IT MATTERS:
  broken             -> somebody with parts
  not working properly -> somebody to check
                          the settings

THEN THREE DETAILS:
  1  what exactly happens
       It stops after about a minute.
  2  when it started
       Since Tuesday. Since the power cut.
  3  what you've already tried
       I've switched it off and on.
grammar.workedExample:
The heating comes on but only warms one room.
1. Does anything happen? Yes — it comes on. So not it doesn't work.
2. Is a part physically damaged? You do not know. So not it's broken.
3. It runs but does the wrong thing. That is it's not working properly.
4. Add the three details: The heating is not working properly — it comes on but only warms the front room. It started on Tuesday. I've bled the radiators already.
That report tells somebody what to bring and stops them suggesting the thing you have done.
Compare the version most people give: the heating's broken. That sends an engineer with parts for a heating system that is, in fact, working.
grammar.commonMistake: Saying broken as a general word for anything wrong. It is the most specific of the five and the most over-used, and it sends the wrong help. The other error is stopping at the first sentence — a fault report without when it started and what you have tried will produce two more exchanges before anybody does anything.
grammar.memoryTip: Broken means a part failed. Not working properly means it does the wrong thing.

6. The printer prints, but everything comes out grey.
grammar.answerKey:
1. It doesn't work.
2. It's broken.
3. It's not working properly.
4. There's something wrong with it.
5. It isn't working.
6. It's not working properly.
Numbers 3 and 6 are the same category and the one people reach for broken instead. In both, the thing is running — it is doing the wrong thing, which is a different problem entirely.
Number 5 uses isn't working rather than doesn't work because it was fine an hour ago, which suggests something temporary.

grammar.title: So that: giving the purpose
grammar.explanation: Unit 13 gave you so for a result. So that gives a purpose — why you want something, what you are trying to achieve. Four extra words that change how much help you get.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
SO THAT = PURPOSE (what you want to happen)
  I'm writing so that you have it in writing.
  I'd like an early appointment so that I
     don't miss work.
  Can you confirm by email so that I have
     a record?

AGAINST UNIT 13's SO = RESULT
  It was raining, so we stayed at home.
     ^ already happened
  I'm leaving early so that I catch the train.
     ^ what I want to happen

THE TEST:
  if IN ORDER TO fits, it's SO THAT
     in order to catch the train        yes
     in order to we stayed at home      no

WHY IT WORKS:
  "Can I have an early appointment?"
     -> can be refused in one word
  "...so that I don't miss work."
     -> "No early ones, but there's a
         late one at six - would that work?"

KEEP IT TO ONE CLAUSE.
  A purpose helps. A long explanation
  makes it harder to say yes.
grammar.workedExample:
You want an appointment that does not cost you a day's pay.
1. What are you asking for? An early appointment. That is your guess at a solution.
2. What is the actual need? Not missing work. That is the purpose.
3. Join them with so that: Could I have an early appointment so that I don't miss work?
4. Notice what you have made possible. If nothing early exists, they can now offer you something late instead, because they know what you are trying to achieve.
Now check it against the Unit 13 word. Could you put in order to there? In order to avoid missing work — yes. So it is so that, not so.
And keep it to one clause. So that I don't miss work is a purpose. Three sentences about your shift pattern is an explanation, and it works against you.
grammar.commonMistake: Using so where so that is needed, or the reverse. So gives a result that already happened; so that gives a purpose that has not. The other error is length: adding a paragraph of explanation instead of one clause. The extra words do not add sympathy — they make the request feel heavier and easier to refuse.
grammar.memoryTip: If in order to fits, use so that. One clause only.
grammar.practice:

5. I'm leaving at six. / I want to catch the last train.
6. Now write one with so instead, showing a result.
grammar.answerKey:
1. I'd like an early appointment so that I don't miss work.
2. Can you confirm by email so that I have a record?
3. I'm writing so that the delay is on file.
4. Could you send it today so that I can submit it before the deadline?
5. I'm leaving at six so that I catch the last train.
6. Model: The part hadn't arrived, so the engineer couldn't finish. — a result, already happened.
Check 1 to 5 with the test: in order to fits in every one. In number 6 it does not, which is how you know that one is a result rather than a purpose.
Every answer is one clause long. If yours ran to two sentences, cut it back — the shorter version is the more effective one.

grammar.title: Forms and appointments
grammar.explanation: Forms are mostly vocabulary, and four instructions catch almost everybody. Appointments have a fixed order, like the ticket window in Unit 10.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
FOUR THINGS THAT GO WRONG ON FORMS

  SURNAME / FIRST NAME
     family name / given name.
     Countries order these differently.
     Read the LABEL, not the position.

  OCCUPATION
     your JOB. Not your employer.

  DELETE AS APPLICABLE
     cross out the ones that DON'T apply.
     You are removing the wrong answers.

  BLOCK CAPITALS
     large separate letters, not joined.

TWO HABITS
  · Read the WHOLE form before writing.
    The last question often changes an
    earlier answer.
  · If a box doesn't apply, write N/A.
    A blank looks like you forgot.

TICK ONE BOX ONLY  vs  TICK ALL THAT APPLY
  These look alike and are opposite.

APPOINTMENTS - the order:
  1 what you need
  2 when you're available
  3 whether it's urgent   <- people omit this
  4 your details
grammar.workedExample:
You are telephoning about a leak under the sink.
1. What you need, first: I'd like to make an appointment about a leak under the kitchen sink.
2. When you are available: I'm available any morning this week.
3. Whether it is urgent — the part people leave out: It's not urgent, but it is getting worse.
4. Your details, last, because they will ask for them anyway.
Step 3 is what decides when you are seen. Not urgent but getting worse is a specific and honest position, and it is treated differently from both this is an emergency and whenever suits you.
Now the form version. The same leak, on the repair form: tick Water, not Other. Tick getting worse under urgency — and note that box says tick all that apply, so you may also tick more than one.
grammar.commonMistake: Treating tick one box only and tick all that apply as the same instruction. They sit close together on most forms and mean opposite things. The other errors are writing your employer under occupation, and leaving boxes blank rather than writing N/A — a blank is indistinguishable from an oversight and the form comes back.
grammar.memoryTip: Read the labels, not the positions. N/A beats blank.

6. Make an appointment about a leak, in the right order.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Your family name.
2. Your job — not your employer.
3. Cross out the options that do not apply to you, leaving the one that does.
4. The first allows exactly one answer; the second allows any number. They look similar and are opposite.
5. N/A. A blank looks like you forgot and the form may be returned.
6. I'd like to make an appointment about a leak under the kitchen sink. I'm available any morning this week. It's not urgent but it is getting worse. My name is …
Check your answer to 6 has all three parts before the details. The urgency line is the one almost everybody omits, and it is the one that decides when you are seen.

2. I'd like an appointment about a door lock that isn't working properly — it works about half the time. I'm available any afternoon. It's not urgent yet, but I'm concerned about being locked out. My name is …
3. I need someone urgently — there's water coming through the ceiling. I'm at home now and can stay in. This is an emergency. My name is …
4. I'd like to book a repair when convenient. I'm flexible on days, mornings are easier. It isn't urgent at all, but I'd like it done this month if possible. My name is …
Every one states the urgency explicitly, including number 4 where the urgency is none — saying so is still useful, because it tells them where you belong on the list.
Numbers 1 and 2 both use not urgent but, which is the most useful frame here: honest, specific, and treated differently from both an emergency and no preference.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Fill in a real form
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Find one real form — paper or online. A registration, an application, a request, anything.
Read the whole thing before writing.
Write down: every instruction you were not certain about, what you decided it meant, and any box where you had to write N/A.
Do not submit anything you were not already going to submit, and do not copy any of your own personal details into your notes.

No key — it is your form.

The second finding is about reading the whole form first. Almost everybody finds one question near the end that would have changed an answer near the beginning — most often a question about circumstances that makes an earlier section not apply.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Report one real fault
activities.instructionsAndItems:
This week, report one real fault to somebody — a landlord, a shop, a service, a colleague.
Use the four-sentence shape: which description, what exactly happens, when it started, what you have already tried.
Write three lines: what you said, what they asked you next, and whether they asked you to try something you had already tried.

No key.
